خط.etymology: Classical Arabic خَطّ (ḫaṭṭ, 'line, mark, furrow; handwriting, calligraphy; telephone or transit line') from خَطَّ (ḫaṭṭa, 'to draw a line, trace, write'), root خ-ط-ط (ḫ-ṭ-ṭ).

خطاب.etymology: Verbal and concrete noun خِطَاب (ḫiṭāb, 'speech, public address, formal letter') from خَاطَبَ (ḫāṭaba, 'to address, speak to'), root خ-ط-ب (ḫ-ṭ-b).

خطة.etymology: Noun خُطَّة (ḫuṭṭa, 'plan, course of action, laid-out design'), originally a plot of land or course marked out with lines, from خَطَّ (ḫaṭṭa, 'to trace lines'), root خ-ط-ط (ḫ-ṭ-ṭ).

خطوة.etymology: Instance noun خَطْوَة (ḫaṭwa, 'a step, pace, footstep') from خَطَا (ḫaṭā, 'to step, walk, pace'), root خ-ط-و (ḫ-ṭ-w).

خطّط.etymology: Form II verb خَطَّطَ (ḫaṭṭaṭa, 'to draw lines, lay out a design, plan') from خَطّ (ḫaṭṭ, 'line'), root خ-ط-ط (ḫ-ṭ-ṭ).

history.meaning: to mark with lines; design; plan

خف.etymology: Form I geminate verb خَفَّ (ḫaffa, 'to be light in weight, become lighter, ease off, subside'), from the Semitic root خ-ف-ف (ḫ-f-f, 'lightness').

history.meaning: to be light; lessen; ease off

خفق.etymology: Form I verb خَفَقَ (ḫafaqa, 'to beat, throb, flutter; in cooking, to whisk or whip eggs and cream until light'), root خ-ف-ق (ḫ-f-q).

خفيف.etymology: Adjective خَفِيف (ḫafīf, 'light in weight, mild, gentle, nimble') on the pattern فَعِيل from خَفَّ (ḫaffa, 'to be light'), root خ-ف-ف (ḫ-f-f).

خفّف.etymology: Form II causative verb خَفَّفَ (ḫaffafa, 'to lighten, reduce, tone down, soften') from خَفَّ (ḫaffa, 'to be light'), root خ-ف-ف (ḫ-f-f).

خل.etymology: Collective noun خَلّ ('vinegar') from the geminate Semitic root خ-ل-ل ('turn sour, ferment acidly'), naming wine or cider soured into household vinegar.

خلاف.etymology: Form III verbal noun خِلَاف (ḫilāf, 'disagreement, difference, variance, dispute') from خَالَفَ (ḫālafa, 'to differ with, go contrary to'), root خ-ل-ف (ḫ-l-f).

خلفي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective خَلْفِيّ (ḫalfiyy, 'back, rear, posterior') formed from خَلْف (ḫalfa, 'behind, at the back of'), root خ-ل-ف (ḫ-l-ف).

خلّص.etymology: Form II verb خَلَّصَ (ḫallaṣa, 'to extricate, clear; [in Levantine] to finish, complete') from خَلَصَ (ḫalaṣa, 'to become pure, clear, finished'), root خ-ل-ص (ḫ-l-ṣ).

history.meaning: to clear; bring to completion; finish

خلّى.etymology: Form II verb خَلَّى (ḫallā, 'to leave alone, vacate; [in Levantine] to let, allow, keep') from خَلَا (ḫalā, 'to be empty, free'), root خ-ل-و (ḫ-l-w).

خمسة.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḫamš- ('five'), yielding Classical Arabic خَمْسَة (ḫamsa), root خ-م-س (ḫ-m-s).

خمستعشر.etymology: Spoken Levantine construct compound numeral خَمْسْتَعْشَر (ḫamstaʿšar, 'fifteen' before a counted noun), contracted from Classical خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ (ḫamsata ʿašara, 'five-teen').

خمسين.etymology: Oblique/generalized spoken form of Classical خَمْسُونَ / خَمْسِينَ (ḫamsīna, 'fifty'), decade numeral formed with the plural suffix -īn from خَمْس ('five'), root خ-م-س.

خيال.etymology: Classical Arabic خَيَال (ḫayāl, 'apparition, silhouette, cast shadow; imagination, fancy') from خَالَ (ḫāla, 'to suppose, imagine'), root خ-ي-ل (ḫ-y-l).

خير.etymology: Classical Arabic خَيْر (ḫayr, 'good, goodness, blessing, well-being'), central to everyday greetings such as صباح الخير ('good morning') and تصبحوا على خير ('good night'), root خ-ي-ر (ḫ-y-r).

خَبَز.etymology: Form I verb خَبَزَ (ḫabaza, 'to bake bread or pastry; vocalized with fatḥas to distinguish the verb from خُبْز "bread" and خَبْز "baking"'), root خ-ب-ز (ḫ-b-z).

خَبْز.etymology: Form I verbal noun خَبْز (ḫabz, 'act of baking; vocalized with fatḥa-sukūn to distinguish it from خُبْز ḫubz "bread"') from خَبَزَ (ḫabaza, 'to bake'), root خ-ب-ز.

خِلِص.etymology: Spoken Levantine Form I intransitive verb خِلِص (ḫiliṣ, 'to run out, be finished, come to an end'), from Classical خَلَصَ (ḫalaṣa, 'to become clear, reach completion'), root خ-ل-ص (ḫ-l-ṣ).

history.meaning: to reach the end; become clear

دائرة.etymology: Feminine active participle substantive دَائِرَة (dāʾira, 'circle, ring; administrative department, bureau') from دَارَ (dāra, 'to go around, revolve'), root د-و-ر (d-w-r).

دائم.etymology: Active participle adjective دَائِم (dāʾim, 'lasting, permanent, continual') from دَامَ (dāma, 'to last, endure, continue'), root د-و-م (d-w-m).

دار.etymology: Hollow verb دَارَ (dāra, 'to turn, go around; [in Levantine, merging with Form IV أَدَارَ ʾadāra] to run, manage a place, or direct attention in دير بالك "take care"'), root د-و-ر (d-w-r).

دافع.etymology: Active participle دَافِع (dāfiʿ, 'pushing; paying, having paid; motive') from دَفَعَ (dafaʿa, 'to push; pay'), root د-ف-ع (d-f-ʿ).

دافي.etymology: Spoken and lightened Classical form دَافِي (dāfī, 'warm, cozy') of دَافِئ (dāfiʾ) via regular loss of final glottal stop, active participle of دَفِئَ (dafiʾa, 'to be warm'), root د-ف-ء (d-f-ʾ).

داق.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with regular shift of interdental ذ ḏ to dental stop د d) of Classical ذَاقَ (ḏāqa, 'to taste, sample food'), root ذ-و-ق (ḏ-w-q).

دايما.etymology: Spoken Levantine form دَايْمًا (dāyman, 'always') with palatal glide y for the Classical medial hamza in دَائِمًا (dāʾiman, 'continually, always'), adverbial accusative of دَائِم (root د-و-م).

دبوس.etymology: Classical and Levantine noun دَبُّوس (dabbūs, 'pin, tack, metal pivot pin; originally a rounded iron mace'), formed on the instrument pattern فَعُّول from root د-ب-س (d-b-s).

history.meaning: knobbed mace; metal pin; pivot pin

دخل.etymology: Form I verb دَخَلَ (daḫala, 'to enter, come in, go inside'), from the Semitic root د-خ-ل (d-ḫ-l, 'entering, interior').

دخيلك.etymology: Warm Levantine entreaty دَخِيلَك (daḫīlak, 'please!, I beg you!'), literally '[I am] your sanctuary-seeker (دَخِيل)', referring to the ancient Arabian custom of entering (دَخَلَ) a host\'s tent to claim protection, root د-خ-ل.

history.meaning: your sanctuary-guest; 'I appeal to your protection!'

دخّل.etymology: Form II causative verb دَخَّلَ (daḫḫala, 'to bring inside, let in, insert') from دَخَلَ (daḫala, 'to enter'), root د-خ-ل (d-ḫ-l).

history.meaning: to cause to enter; bring inside

درج.etymology: From the root د-ر-ج (d-r-j, 'to step, advance gradually'), used collectively for a flight of stairs—or with different vowels (دُرج) for a desk drawer.
درج.notes: Amman's hillsides are famous for public stone staircases (أدراج) linking upper and lower streets.

درجة.etymology: Noun دَرَجَة (daraja, 'step, stair, rung; degree, grade') from دَرَجَ (daraja, 'to walk step by step, advance by degrees'), root د-ر-ج (d-r-j).

درس.etymology: Verbal and concrete noun دَرْس (dars, 'studying; lesson, class') from دَرَسَ (darasa, 'to study, read repeatedly'), cognate with Aramaic דְּרַשׁ (daraš, 'to expound, study'), root د-ر-س (d-r-s).

درفة.etymology: Levantine and Egyptian architectural noun دَرْفَة (darfa, 'single hinged leaf or panel of a double window, shutter, or door'), from Classical دَرْف (darf, 'side, wing, protective screen'), root د-ر-ف (d-r-f).

history.meaning: side wing; hinged shutter or door leaf

دزينة.etymology: Levantine market noun دَزِّينَة (dazzīne, 'dozen, set of twelve'), borrowed from Italian dozzina ('dozen', ultimately from Latin duodecim 'twelve').

دعا.etymology: Form I verb دَعَا (daʿā, 'to call, invite; pray for someone, wish someone well') from the Semitic root د-ع-و (d-ʿ-w, 'calling, invoking').

دغري.etymology: Signature Levantine adverb دُغْرِي (duġrī, 'straight ahead; right away, directly; honest'), borrowed from Ottoman Turkish doğru ('straight, direct, true, right').

دفا.etymology: Spoken and lightened Classical noun دَفَا (dafā, 'warmth') from Classical دِفْء / دَفَاء (difʾ / dafāʾ, 'warmth, shelter from cold') via regular loss of final glottal stop, root د-ف-ء (d-f-ʾ).

دفاية.etymology: Appliance noun دَفَّايَة (daffāye, 'heater, radiator, stove') on the instrumental pattern فَعَّالَة from دَفَّى < دَفَّأَ (daffaʾa, 'to warm, heat'), root د-ف-ء (d-f-ʾ).

دفتر.etymology: Borrowed via Persian *daftar* from Ancient Greek διφθέρα (diphthéra, 'prepared hide, parchment, ledger').
دفتر.notes: Entered Classical Arabic early for an account register or ledger—just like Tariq's paper reception book.

دفع.etymology: Form I verb دَفَعَ (dafaʿa, 'to push, propel, ward off; hand over a sum, pay'), from the Semitic root د-ف-ع (d-f-ʿ).

دفن.etymology: Form I verb دَفَنَ (dafana, 'to bury, conceal in the earth'), from the Semitic root د-ف-ن (d-f-n, 'burying, covering over').

history.meaning: to bury; cover in the ground

دق.etymology: Form I geminate verb دَقَّ (daqqa, 'to knock, beat, pound, chime'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *daqaq- ('to beat fine, pound'), root د-ق-ق (d-q-q).

دقة.etymology: Covers both the instance noun دَقَّة (daqqa, 'a single knock, beat, or clock chime') and the abstract noun دِقَّة (diqqa, 'fineness, accuracy, precision, punctuality'), from the geminate root د-ق-ق (d-q-q).

history.meaning: single knock or chime; precision, exactness

دقيقة.etymology: Feminine noun دَقِيقَة (daqīqa, 'minute [of time or arc]'), literally 'a fine or small part' (paralleled by Medieval Latin pars minuta prima, 'first small division of the hour'), from دَقِيق (daqīq, 'fine, minute'), root د-ق-ق.

history.meaning: minute particle; minute (sixtieth of an hour)

دكان.etymology: Classical Arabic دُكَّان (dukkān, 'raised platform or bench; shop, store'), borrowed in antiquity via Aramaic דֻּכָּנָא (dukkānā) from Akkadian dukkannu / Sumerian dug-gan ('platform, counter').

دلف.etymology: Verbal and concrete noun دَلْف (dalf, 'roof leak, dripping of rainwater through a ceiling') from دَلَفَ (dalafa, 'to trickle, leak through a roof'), cognate with Aramaic דְּלַף / ܕܠܦ (dalap̄, 'to drip, leak'), root د-ل-ف (d-l-f).

دليل.etymology: Noun دَلِيل (dalīl, 'guide, guidebook, indicator, sign, proof') on the pattern فَعِيل from دَلَّ (dalla, 'to point out, guide, direct'), root د-ل-ل (d-l-l).

دم.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *dam- ('blood'), one of the core biradical anatomical nouns across all Semitic languages, yielding Classical Arabic دَم (dam).

دندن.etymology: Expressive reduplicated quadriliteral verb دَنْدَنَ (dandana, 'to hum a tune softly, murmur, buzz'), formed onomatopoeically on the root د-ن-د-ن (d-n-d-n).

دندنة.etymology: Quadriliteral verbal noun دَنْدَنَة (dandana, 'soft humming of a melody, gentle strumming or murmuring') from دَنْدَنَ (dandana, 'to hum'), root د-ن-د-ن.

دنيا.etymology: Feminine elative substantive دُنْيَا (dunyā, 'this world, earthly life; [in Levantine] the world and weather outside'), originally feminine of أَدْنَى (ʾadnā, 'nearer, closer', i.e. '[the] nearer life'), from دَنَا ('to be near'), root د-ن-و (d-n-w).

دهان.etymology: Verbal and material noun دِهَان (dihān, 'paint, oil coating, pigment; act of painting') from دَهَنَ (dahana, 'to oil, anoint, coat with paint'), root د-ه-ن (d-h-n).

دهبي.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with regular shift of interdental ذ ḏ to stop د d) of Classical ذَهَبِيّ (ḏahabiyy, 'golden, gold-colored'), nisba adjective from ذَهَب (ḏahab, 'gold', Proto-Semitic *ḏahab-), root ذ-ه-ب.

دهن.etymology: Form I verb دَهَنَ (dahana, 'to anoint, oil, coat, paint walls or woodwork'), from the Semitic root د-ه-ن (d-h-n, 'oil, grease, coating').

دو.etymology: Musical solfège syllable دُو (dō, 'the note C'), borrowed from Italian/French do (which replaced earlier ut in European solfège).

history.meaning: first note of the diatonic scale (C)

دواسة.etymology: Instrumental noun دَوَّاسَة (dawwāsa, 'foot pedal, piano pedal, treadle, doormat') on the pattern فَعَّالَة from دَاسَ (dāsa, 'to tread, step on, press with the foot'), root د-و-س (d-w-s).

دوام.etymology: Verbal noun دَوَام (dawām, 'continuance, permanence; regular working hours, work shift') from دَامَ (dāma, 'to last, continue, endure'), root د-و-م (d-w-m).

دور.etymology: Verbal and concrete noun دَوْر (dawr, 'rotation, cycle, turn; role or part; story/floor of a building') from دَارَ (dāra, 'to turn, revolve'), root د-و-ر (d-w-r).

دوزان.etymology: Levantine and Egyptian musical term دُوزَان (dūzān, 'tuning of a stringed or keyboard instrument'), borrowed from Ottoman Turkish düzen ('order, harmony, musical tuning', from Turkic düz- 'to arrange, put in order').

دوزن.etymology: Levantine quadriliteral verb دَوْزَن (dawzan, 'to tune a musical instrument'), denominalized from دُوزَان (dūzān, 'musical tuning', from Ottoman Turkish düzen).

دوش.etymology: Household noun دُوش (dūš, 'bath shower'), borrowed from French douche ('shower', itself from Italian doccia 'water conduit, spout').

دوّر.etymology: Form II verb دَوَّرَ (dawwara, 'to turn round, make revolve; [with عَلَى] to go around looking for, search for') from دَارَ (dāra, 'to turn, go around'), root د-و-ر (d-w-r).

history.meaning: to turn round; search for (with على)

دينار.etymology: Classical Arabic دِينَار (dīnār, 'gold coin; modern currency unit of Jordan and several Arab countries'), borrowed in antiquity via Aramaic/Syriac ܕܝܢܪܐ (dīnārā) and Greek δηνάριον from Latin dēnārius ('coin of ten asses').

ذان.etymology: Colloquial Jordanian and Levantine noun ذَان / دَان (ḏān / dān, 'ear'), back-formed as a long-vowel singular from the Classical broken plural آذَان (ʾāḏān, 'ears', plural of أُذُن ʾuḏun), root ء-ذ-ن.

ذكرى.etymology: Feminine noun ذِكْرَى (ḏikrā, 'memory, remembrance, recollection, commemoration') formed with the feminine suffix -َى (-ā) on the pattern فِعْلَى from ذَكَرَ (ḏakara, 'to remember, mention'), root ذ-ك-ر.

ذكي.etymology: Adjective ذَكِيّ (ḏakiyy, 'smart, clever, quick-witted') on the pattern فَعِيل from ذَكَا (ḏakā, 'to blaze brightly [of fire], give off a sharp scent, be acute in mind'), root ذ-ك-و (ḏ-k-w).

ذكّر.etymology: Form II causative verb ذَكَّرَ (ḏakkara, 'to remind, cause to remember') from ذَكَرَ (ḏakara, 'to remember'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḏakar-, root ذ-ك-ر.

ذواق.etymology: Intensive agent noun ذَوَّاق (ḏawwāq, 'taste-tester, connoisseur, person of refined palate') on the pattern فَعَّال from ذَاقَ (ḏāqa, 'to taste'), root ذ-و-ق (ḏ-w-q).

ذوق.etymology: Form I verbal noun ذَوْق (ḏawq, 'sense of taste; good taste, tact, grace, kindness', as in كلك ذوق 'you are all kindness') from ذَاقَ (ḏāqa, 'to taste'), root ذ-و-ق (ḏ-w-q).

رئيسي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective رَئِيسِيّ (raʾīsiyy, 'main, principal, chief, primary') derived from رَئِيس (raʾīs, 'chief, head'), from رَأْس (raʾs, 'head'), root ر-ء-س (r-ʾ-s).

رائع.etymology: Active participle adjective رَائِع (rāʾiʿ, 'wonderful, splendid, admirable, striking') from رَاعَ (rāʿa, 'to strike with awe, dazzle, thrill with admiration'), root ر-و-ع (r-w-ʿ).

رابع.etymology: Ordinal adjective رَابِع (rābiʿ, 'fourth') formed on the pattern فَاعِل from أَرْبَعَة (ʾarbaʿa, 'four'), root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ).

راتب.etymology: From the triliteral root ر-ت-ب (r-t-b), expressing steadiness, order, and fixed arrangement. As an active participle راتب describes something regular and enduring, whence a fixed periodic salary.
راتب.notes: Used across modern Arabic for a regular monthly wage alongside مرتب.

راجع.etymology: Active participle رَاجِع (rājiʿ, 'returning, coming back') from رَجَعَ (rajaʿa, 'to return'), root ر-ج-ع (r-j-ʿ).

راح.etymology: Hollow Form I verb رَاحَ (rāḥa, 'to go, depart, be gone'), originally in Classical Arabic 'to go or travel in the cool evening breeze [رَوَاح]', generalized in spoken Arabic as the primary verb 'to go', root ر-و-ح (r-w-ḥ).

history.meaning: to set out in the evening; go; depart

راحة.etymology: Noun رَاحَة (rāḥa, 'rest, repose, comfort, ease') from the Semitic root ر-و-ح (r-w-ḥ, 'refreshing breeze, breath, relief from toil').

راس.etymology: Spoken and lightened Classical form رَاس (rās, 'head, top, summit') of رَأْس (raʾs) via compensatory lengthening after loss of medial glottal stop, inherited from Proto-Semitic *raʾš- ('head'), root ر-ء-س.

راضي.etymology: Active participle رَاضٍ / الرَّاضِي (rāḍī, 'satisfied, content, willing; [with مش] unwilling, refusing to budge') from رَضِيَ (raḍiya, 'to be pleased, consent'), root ر-ض-و / ر-ض-ي.

راقب.etymology: Form III verb رَاقَبَ (rāqaba, 'to watch closely, observe, monitor, keep an eye on') from رَقَبَ (raqaba, 'to watch, look out'), connected to رَقَبَة ('neck, stretched to look out'), root ر-ق-ب (r-q-b).

راقص.etymology: Active participle adjective رَاقِص (rāqiṣ, 'dancing, lilting') from رَقَصَ (raqaṣa, 'to dance, leap rhythmicaly'), root ر-ق-ص (r-q-ṣ).

رايح.etymology: Spoken Levantine active participle رَايِح (rāyiḥ, 'going, heading to') with palatal glide y for the Classical medial hamza in رَائِح (rāʾiḥ), active participle of رَاحَ ('to go'), root ر-و-ح.

رب.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *rabb- ('great, chief, master, lord'), yielding Classical Arabic رَبّ (rabb, 'Lord, master'), root ر-ب-ب (r-b-b).

ربع.etymology: Fractional noun رُبْع (rubʿ, 'one-fourth, quarter; fifteen minutes of an hour') formed on the fractional pattern فُعْل from the numeral root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ, 'four').

ربيع.etymology: From the root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ), connected with resting in lush pasture and spring rains that revive grazing land; hence the spring season across Arabic dialects.

رتّب.etymology: Form II verb رَتَّبَ (rattaba, 'to arrange, put in order, tidy') from رَتَبَ (rataba, 'to stand firm and upright in rank'), root ر-ت-ب (r-t-b).

history.meaning: to arrange; put in order; tidy

رجا.etymology: Form I verb رَجَا (rajā, 'to hope for, entreat, ask earnestly', used in the polite request أَرْجُوك ʾarjūk 'please! / I beg you'), from the root ر-ج-و (r-j-w).

رجال.etymology: Spoken Levantine singular noun رِجَّال (rijjāl, 'man'), reshaped on the intensive pattern فِعَّال from Classical Arabic رَجُل (rajul, 'man', originally 'man on foot', plural رِجَال rijāl), root ر-ج-ل.

رجالي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective رِجَالِيّ (rijāliyy, 'men\'s, for men') formed from the broken plural رِجَال (rijāl, 'men', plural of رَجُل), root ر-ج-ل (r-j-l).

رجع.etymology: Form I verb رَجَعَ (rajaʿa, 'to return, come back, go back'), from the root ر-ج-ع (r-j-ʿ).

رجعة.etymology: Instance noun (ism marra) رَجْعَة (rajʿa, 'a return, return trip, coming back') from رَجَعَ (rajaʿa, 'to return'), root ر-ج-ع (r-j-ʿ).

رجف.etymology: Form I verb رَجَفَ (rajafa, 'to tremble, shake, shiver, quake'), from the Semitic root ر-ج-ف (r-j-f, 'quaking, trembling').

رجل.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *rigl- ('foot, leg'), yielding Classical Arabic رِجْل (rijl), a core feminine paired body-part noun, root ر-ج-ل (r-j-l).

رجّع.etymology: Form II causative verb رَجَّعَ (rajjaʿa, 'to bring back, return [something], restore') from رَجَعَ (rajaʿa, 'to come back'), root ر-ج-ع (r-j-ʿ).

history.meaning: to cause to return; bring back; give back

رح.etymology: Spoken Levantine invariant future particle رَح (raḥ, 'will, going to'), grammaticalized by phonetic reduction from the active participle رَايِح (rāyiḥ < رَائِح, 'going [to]'), root ر-و-ح.

رحلة.etymology: Noun رِحْلَة (riḥla, 'trip, journey, travel') from رَحَلَ (raḥala, 'to saddle a mount, set out on a journey'), root ر-ح-ل (r-ḥ-l).

رحم.etymology: Form I verb رَحِمَ (raḥima, 'to have mercy, compassion on'), inherited from the Proto-Semitic root ر-ح-م (*r-ḥ-m, 'womb; tender mercy, compassion').

رخامة.etymology: Singulative noun رُخَامَة (ruḫāma, 'a slab of marble; in Levantine households, the kitchen countertop') from the Classical collective رُخَام (ruḫām, 'marble'), root ر-خ-م (r-ḫ-m).

رخّى.etymology: Spoken Levantine Form II verb رَخَّى (raḫḫā, 'to loosen, slacken, ease tension'), corresponding to Classical Form IV أَرْخَى (ʾarḫā) from رَخُوَ (raḫuwa, 'to be soft, loose, slack'), root ر-خ-و (r-ḫ-w).

رد.etymology: Form I geminate verb رَدَّ (radda, 'to send back, turn back; reply, answer a call or question'), from the Semitic root ر-د-د (r-d-d, 'returning, replying').

history.meaning: to return; send back; answer, reply

رسالة.etymology: Derived on pattern فِعَالَة from root ر-س-ل (r-s-l, 'to send forth a messenger or dispatch'): anything sent, from a handwritten letter to a recorded voice message.

رسم.etymology: Form I verb رَسَمَ (rasama, 'to trace, mark out, draw, sketch'), cognate with Aramaic רְשַׁם (rəšam, 'to inscribe, trace, draw'), root ر-س-م (r-s-m).

history.meaning: to trace; mark out; draw; sketch

رسمة.etymology: Instance and concrete noun رَسْمَة (rasma, 'a drawing, sketch, design') from رَسَمَ (rasama, 'to draw, sketch'), root ر-س-م (r-s-m).

رسمي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective رَسْمِيّ (rasmiyy, 'official, formal, prescribed') derived from رَسْم (rasm, 'prescribed mark, established rule or canon'), root ر-س-م (r-s-m).

رسميا.etymology: Adverbial accusative رَسْمِيًّا (rasmiyyan, 'officially, formally') from the relational adjective رَسْمِيّ (rasmiyy, 'official'), root ر-س-م (r-s-m).

رش.etymology: Form I geminate verb رَشَّ (rašša, 'to sprinkle, splash, spray water or fine powder'), inherited from the Semitic root ر-ش-ش (r-š-š, 'sprinkling, light rain').

رشة.etymology: Instance noun رَشَّة (rašša, 'a sprinkle, light spray, or culinary pinch [of salt/spice]') from رَشَّ (rašša, 'to sprinkle, spray'), root ر-ش-ش (r-š-š).

رشفة.etymology: Instance noun رَشْفَة (rašfa, 'a sip, small draught') from رَشَفَ (rašafa, 'to sip gently with the lips'), root ر-ش-ف (r-š-f).

رصاص.etymology: Classical Arabic material noun رَصَاص (raṣāṣ / ruṣāṣ, 'lead, tin'), associated with root ر-ص-ص ('to press tightly together, solder with lead'); paired with قلم in قلم رصاص ('lead pencil').

رصيف.etymology: Noun رَصِيف (raṣīf, 'paved stone causeway, sidewalk, pavement, railway platform, quay') on the passive-sense pattern فَعِيل ('that which is fitted tightly stone-to-stone') from رَصَفَ (raṣafa, 'to lay stones closely together'), root ر-ص-ف (r-ṣ-ف).

رطب.etymology: Adjective رَطْب (raṭb, 'moist, damp, wet, fresh') from رَطُبَ (raṭuba, 'to be moist, tender, fresh'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *raṭb- ('moist, green'), root ر-ط-ب.

رطوبة.etymology: Abstract quality noun رُطُوبَة ('dampness, moisture, humidity') formed on the pattern فُعُولَة from the root ر-ط-ب ('be moist, fresh, tender').

رف.etymology: Classical Arabic رَفّ (raff, 'wall shelf, ledge, bracket', plural رُفُوف rufūf), from the geminate root ر-ف-ف (r-f-f).

رفع.etymology: Form I verb رَفَعَ (rafaʿa, 'to lift, raise, elevate'), from the Semitic root ر-ف-ع (r-f-ʿ, 'lifting, raising high').

رفيع.etymology: Adjective رَفِيع (rafīʿ, 'high in rank; fine in thread or texture, thin, slender') on the pattern فَعِيل from رَفُعَ (rafuʿa, 'to be elevated, fine, slender'), root ر-ف-ع (r-f-ʿ).

رقم.etymology: Classical Arabic رَقْم (raqm > spoken raqam, 'written mark, figure, numeral, number') from رَقَمَ (raqama, 'to mark, stripe, inscribe'), root ر-ق-م (r-q-m).

رقيق.etymology: Adjective رَقِيق (raqīq, 'thin, fine, delicate, tender') on the pattern فَعِيل from رَقَّ (raqqa, 'to be thin, delicate, gentle'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *raqīq- ('thin'), root ر-ق-ق.

ركب.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *rakib- ('to mount, ride, sit upon'), yielding Classical Arabic رَكِبَ (rakiba, 'to ride, board a vehicle; fit upon'), root ر-ك-ب (r-k-b).

history.meaning: to mount; ride; fit in place

ركبة.etymology: Anatomical noun رُكْبَة (rukba, 'knee', plural رُكَب rukab), inherited from Proto-Semitic *birk- / *rukb-at- ('knee', with consonant metathesis in Arabic), root ر-ك-ب.

ركض.etymology: Form I verbal noun رَكْض (rakḍ, 'running, sprinting, galloping') from رَكَضَ (rakaḍa, 'to run, urge a mount with the foot'), root ر-ك-ض (r-k-ḍ).

ركضة.etymology: Instance noun (ism marra) رَكْضَة (rakḍa, 'a run, sprint, quick dash') from رَكَضَ (rakaḍa, 'to run'), root ر-ك-ض (r-k-ḍ).

ركّب.etymology: Form II causative verb رَكَّبَ (rakkaba, 'to mount, fit together, assemble, install') from رَكِبَ (rakiba, 'to mount, sit upon'), root ر-ك-ب (r-k-b).

رمادي.etymology: Relational (nisba) color adjective رَمَادِيّ (ramādiyy, 'ash-colored, grey') derived from رَمَاد (ramād, 'ashes') + -ِيّ (-iyy), root ر-م-د (r-m-d).

رمى.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ramay- ('to throw, cast, shoot'), yielding Classical Arabic رَمَى (ramā, 'to throw, toss, fling'), root ر-م-ي (r-m-y).

رن.etymology: Form I geminate verb رَنَّ (ranna, 'to ring, chime, resound, twang'), inherited from the Semitic expressive root ر-ن-ن (r-n-n, 'ringing, resounding voice or tone').

رنة.etymology: Instance noun (ism marra) رَنَّة (ranna, 'a single ring, chime, or resonant tone') from رَنَّ (ranna, 'to ring'), root ر-ن-ن (r-n-n).

رهيب.etymology: Adjective رَهِيب (rahīb, 'awe-inspiring, formidable; in everyday Levantine speech, terrific, amazing, intense') on the pattern فَعِيل from رَهِبَ (rahiba, 'to stand in awe, fear'), root ر-ه-ب (r-h-b).

روّق.etymology: Form II verb رَوَّقَ (rawwaqa, 'to clarify a liquid; in Levantine, to calm down, relax, clear one\'s mind') from رَاقَ (rāqa, 'to become clear, pure, serene'), root ر-و-ق (r-w-q).

history.meaning: to clarify; make serene; calm down

ري.etymology: Musical solfège syllable رِي (rē, 'the note D'), borrowed from Italian/French ré (second degree of the diatonic scale).

history.meaning: second note of the diatonic scale (D)

ريحة.etymology: Spoken Levantine feminine noun رِيحَة (rīḥa, 'smell, scent, aroma'), formed as a singulative of رِيح (rīḥ, 'wind, breath, odor') and converging with Classical رَائِحَة (rāʾiḥa, 'scent, fragrance'), root ر-و-ح (r-w-ḥ).

رَكَض.etymology: Form I verb رَكَضَ (rakaḍa, 'to run, sprint; vocalized with fatḥas to distinguish the verb from the verbal noun رَكْض'), from the root ر-ك-ض (r-k-ḍ).

زاكي.etymology: Signature Jordanian and Palestinian adjective زَاكِي (zākī, 'delicious, tasty, sweet-smelling'), from Classical زَاكٍ / الزَّاكِي ('pure, thriving, fragrant'), active participle of زَكَا (zakā, 'to thrive, be pure and sweet'), root ز-ك-و (z-k-w).

زان.etymology: Classical and Levantine timber noun زَان (zān, 'beech tree, beechwood'), borrowed via Persian زَان (zān, 'beech tree').

زاوية.etymology: Feminine active-participle substantive زَاوِيَة (zāwiya, 'corner, angle, nook') from زَوَى (zawā, 'to draw together, gather into a corner'), root ز-و-ي (z-w-y).

زبدة.etymology: Singulative and mass noun زُبْدَة (zubda, 'butter, cream; choicest part') from Classical زُبْد (zubd, 'churned butter'), from زَبَدَ (zabada, 'to churn milk into butter'), root ز-ب-د (z-b-d).

زبدية.etymology: Household noun زَبْدِيَّة (zabdiyya, 'ceramic or glass soup/dessert bowl'), formed with the relational suffix -ِيَّة (-iyya) from زُبْد / زَبَد ('butter, cream; glazed earthenware bowl'), root ز-ب-د.

زبط.etymology: Spoken Levantine noun زَبْط (zabṭ, 'exactness, accuracy', especially in بالزبط 'spot-on, exactly'), reflecting the urban sibilant pronunciation of Classical ضَبْط (ḍabṭ, 'precision, holding fast'), root ض-ب-ط.

زحلق.etymology: Expressive quadriliteral verb زَحْلَقَ (zaḥlaqa, 'to slip, slide, skid on a smooth or wet surface'), blended/extended from the Semitic roots ز-ح-ل (z-ḥ-l, 'to slip away, budge') and ز-ل-ق (z-l-q, 'to slip, glide').

زحمة.etymology: Instance/verbal noun زَحْمَة (zaḥma, 'crowd, throng, congestion, rush') from زَحَمَ (zaḥama, 'to press, crowd, jostle'), root ز-ح-م (z-ḥ-m).

زرع.etymology: Verbal and collective noun زَرْع (zarʿ, 'sown crops, plants, greenery') from زَرَعَ (zaraʿa, 'to sow, plant'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḏaraʿ- ('seed, sowing'), root ز-ر-ع.

زعلان.etymology: Adjective زَعْلَان (zaʿlān, 'upset, sad, cross, displeased') formed on the emotional-state pattern فَعْلَان from زَعِلَ (zaʿila, 'to feel vexed, upset'), root ز-ع-ل (z-ʿ-l).

زقاق.etymology: Classical Arabic زُقَاق (zuqāq, 'narrow street, lane, alley'), root ز-ق-ق (z-q-q).

زمان.etymology: Classical Arabic زَمَان (zamān, 'time, era, epoch; in Levantine, long ago, old times'), borrowed in antiquity via Aramaic זְמָנָא (zəmānā) from Old Persian jamāna / Akkadian simānu ('appointed time, season'), root ز-م-ن.

زوج.etymology: Classical Arabic زَوْج (zawj, 'one of a pair, mate, spouse, husband; dual زَوْجَيْن a couple/pair'), borrowed in antiquity via Aramaic זַוְגָא (zawgā) from Ancient Greek ζεῦγος (zeûgos, 'yoke, pair, couple'), root ز-و-ج.

زي.etymology: Spoken Levantine and Egyptian similative preposition زَيّ (zayy, 'like, just as'), grammaticalized from the Classical noun زِيّ (ziyy, 'guise, form, outward appearance, manner').

زيادة.etymology: Form I verbal noun زِيَادَة (ziyāda, 'increase, addition, surplus, extra') from زَادَ (zāda, 'to increase, grow, exceed'), root ز-ي-د (z-y-d).

زيارة.etymology: Form I verbal noun زِيَارَة (ziyāra, 'visit, visiting') from زَارَ (zāra, 'to visit'), root ز-و-ر (z-w-r).

زيت.etymology: Primary noun زَيْت ('oil, originally olive oil'), an ancient Mediterranean-Semitic Wanderwort tied to زَيْتُون ('olive tree/fruit'). Passed from Arabic into Iberian Romance as Spanish aceite and Portuguese azeite.

history.meaning: olive oil; cooking or lubricating oil

زيتون.etymology: Collective noun زَيْتُون ('olives; olive trees'), formed on زَيْت with the Semitic suffix ـُون. Borrowed directly from Arabic (الزَّيْتُونَة) into Spanish aceituna and Portuguese azeitona.

زَرَع.etymology: Form I verb زَرَعَ (zaraʿa, 'to plant, sow, grow; vocalized with fatḥas to distinguish the verb from the noun زَرْع'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḏaraʿ- ('to scatter seed, sow'), root ز-ر-ع.

سأل.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šaʾal- ('to ask, inquire'), yielding Classical Arabic سَأَلَ (saʾala), root س-ء-ل (s-ʾ-l).

ساتر.etymology: Active participle سَاتِر (sātir, 'veiling, shielding; Protector, as a divine attribute invoked in the exclamation يَا سَاتِر! "goodness! / heaven protect us!"') from سَتَرَ (satara, 'to cover, shield'), root س-ت-ر (s-t-r).

ساحة.etymology: From the hollow root س-و-ح (s-w-h, 'to spread out openly'), naming an open inner courtyard or public town square.
ساحة.notes: Traditional Amman houses organize rooms around a sheltered stone ساحة planted with trees and jasmine.

ساعاتي.etymology: Traditional Eastern Mediterranean craft noun سَاعَاتِيّ ('watchmaker, clockmaker'), formed by attaching the Ottoman Turkish occupational suffix -ci (adapted into Levantine Arabic after plural ساعات as ـاتي) to سَاعَة ('clock, watch').

ساعة.etymology: Classical Arabic noun meaning 'a short span of time, moment, hour', later extended to timepieces—both a wall clock (ساعة حيط) and a wristwatch.
ساعة.notes: Used in telling clock time across all varieties of Arabic.

ساعد.etymology: Form III verb سَاعَدَ (sāʿada, 'to help, assist'), denominative from سَاعِد (sāʿid, 'forearm'), meaning literally 'to join one\'s arm alongside another\'s', root س-ع-د (s-ʿ-d).

history.meaning: to lend a hand; help; assist

ساعي.etymology: Active participle noun سَاعٍ / السَّاعِي (sāʿī, 'runner, messenger, courier', especially in سَاعِي البَرِيد 'postman, mail carrier') from سَعَى (saʿā, 'to walk briskly, strive, run errands'), root س-ع-ي (s-ʿ-y).

ساكت.etymology: Active participle adjective سَاكِت (sākit, 'silent, quiet, saying nothing') from سَكَتَ (sakata, 'to fall silent'), root س-ك-ت (s-k-t).

ساكن.etymology: Active participle سَاكِن (sākin, 'dwelling, residing, living in a place; still, motionless') from سَكَنَ (sakana, 'to dwell, be still'), root س-ك-ن (s-k-n).

سالفة.etymology: Jordanian and Arabian noun سَالِفَة (sālifa, plural سَوَالِف / سَوَالِيف sawālīf, 'story, anecdote, friendly chat'), originally the feminine active participle of سَلَفَ (salafa, 'to go before, happen in past times'), root س-ل-ف (s-l-f).

سامع.etymology: Active participle سَامِع (sāmiʿ, 'hearing, listening') from سَمِعَ (samiʿa, 'to hear'), root س-م-ع (s-m-ʿ).

سبب.etymology: Classical Arabic سَبَب (sabab, 'reason, cause, means', originally a tent rope or cord connecting two things), from the root س-ب-ب (s-b-b).

سبعة.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šabʿ- ('seven'), yielding Classical Arabic سَبْعَة (sabʿa), root س-ب-ع (s-b-ʿ).

سبق.etymology: Form I verb سَبَقَ (sabaqa, 'to precede, come before, beat or get ahead of someone'), from the root س-ب-ق (s-b-q).

history.meaning: to precede; outstrip; get ahead of

سبيل.etymology: Classical Arabic سَبِيل (sabīl, 'way, road, path; charitable public drinking-water fountain endowed for wayfarers [ابْن السَّبِيل]'), inherited from Central Semitic *šabīl- ('path, way'), root س-ب-ل.

history.meaning: way; path; charitable public water fountain

ست.etymology: Respectful Levantine and Egyptian title سِتّ (sitt, 'lady, madam, Mrs.; grandmother'), contracted in medieval Arabic from سَيِّدَتِي (sayyidatī, 'my lady'), feminine of سَيِّد ('lord, master'), root س-و-د (s-w-d).

history.meaning: lady; mistress of the house; madam

ستارة.etymology: Noun سِتَارَة (sitāra, 'curtain, drape, screen') on the pattern فِعَالَة from سَتَرَ (satara, 'to veil, cover, screen'), root س-ت-ر (s-t-r).

ستة.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šiḏṯ- ('six'), with assimilation of the medial cluster to -tt- in Classical Arabic سِتَّة (sitta; compare ordinal سَادِس and root س-د-س).

سجادة.etymology: Singulative and instrument noun سَجَّادَة (sajjāda, 'prayer rug, carpet, rug') on the pattern فَعَّالَة from سَجَدَ (sajada, 'to bow down, prostrate oneself in worship'), root س-ج-د (s-j-d).

سجّل.etymology: Form II verb سَجَّلَ (sajjala, 'to register, record, write down in a ledger'), denominative from سِجِلّ (sijill, 'scroll, official register', borrowed via Byzantine Greek σιγίλλιον from Latin sigillum 'seal').

history.meaning: to register; record; enter in a log

سحاب.etymology: Instrument noun سَحَّاب (saḥḥāb, 'zipper, slide fastener') on the pattern فَعَّال ('that which pulls shut') from سَحَبَ (saḥaba, 'to pull, draw'), root س-ح-ب (s-ḥ-b).

سحب.etymology: Form I verb سَحَبَ (saḥaba, 'to pull, draw, drag; withdraw'), from the Semitic root س-ح-ب (s-ḥ-b).

سحري.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective سِحْرِيّ (siḥriyy, 'magical, enchanting') derived from سِحْر (siḥr, 'magic, enchantment'), root س-ح-ر (s-ḥ-r).

سخان.etymology: Appliance noun سَخَّان (saḫḫān, 'water heater, boiler, kettle') on the instrumental pattern فَعَّال from سَخَّنَ (saḫḫana, 'to heat, make hot'), root س-خ-ن (s-ḫ-n).

سخن.etymology: Adjective سُخْن (suḫn > spoken suḫun, 'hot, warm') from سَخُنَ (saḫuna, 'to be hot, warm'), inherited from the Proto-Semitic root س-خ-ن (*š-ḫ-n, 'to be warm, hot').

سدة.etymology: Traditional Levantine architectural noun سُدَّة / سِدَّة (sidde, 'overhead storage loft, mezzanine shelf or gallery'), from Classical سُدَّة (sudda, 'portico, threshold, raised bench'), root س-د-د (s-d-d).

history.meaning: portico; raised platform; overhead storage loft

سر.etymology: Classical Arabic سِرّ (sirr, 'secret, mystery, innermost thought,' plural أَسْرَار ʾasrār), from the geminate root س-ر-ر (s-r-r, 'concealing within the heart').

سرعة.etymology: Abstract noun سُرْعَة (surʿa, 'speed, swiftness, quickness') on the pattern فُعْلَة from سَرُعَ (saruʿa, 'to be swift, fast'), root س-ر-ع (s-r-ʿ).

سرور.etymology: Verbal noun سُرُور (surūr, 'joy, pleasure, delight', as in بِكُلِّ سُرُور 'with pleasure!') from سَرَّ (sarra, 'to gladden, delight'), root س-ر-ر (s-r-r).

سري.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective سِرِّيّ (sirriyy, 'secret, confidential, hidden') derived from سِرّ (sirr, 'secret') + -ِيّ (-iyy), root س-ر-ر.

سريع.etymology: Adjective سَرِيع (sarīʿ, 'fast, quick, swift') on the pattern فَعِيل from سَرُعَ (saruʿa, 'to be fast'), root س-ر-ع (s-r-ʿ).

سطاش.etymology: Spoken compound numeral سِطَّاش (siṭṭāš, 'sixteen'), contracted from Classical سِتَّةَ عَشَرَ (sittata ʿašara, 'six-teen') with emphatic ṭṭ induced by pharyngeal ʿayn.

سطح.etymology: Classical Arabic سَطْح (saṭḥ, 'flat roof, rooftop terrace, upper surface') from سَطَحَ (saṭaḥa, 'to spread out flat, level'), root س-ط-ح (s-ṭ-ḥ).

سطر.etymology: Classical Arabic سَطْر (saṭr, 'line of writing, row') from سَطَرَ (saṭara, 'to rule lines, write, inscribe'), inherited from Ancient Semitic *šaṭār- ('to write', cognate with Akkadian šaṭāru), root س-ط-ر.

history.meaning: ruled line; line of text; row

سطل.etymology: Early Mediterranean loanword سَطْل ('bucket, pail', plural سُطُول), borrowed via Aramaic/Byzantine Greek σίτλα from Latin situla ('water bucket'). Still the everyday word for a bucket across Jordan, Palestine, Syria, and Lebanon.

سعر.etymology: Classical Arabic سِعْر (siʿr, 'price, market rate, valuation'), from the root س-ع-ر (s-ʿ-r).

سعيد.etymology: Adjective سَعِيد (saʿīd, 'happy, fortunate, auspicious') on the pattern فَعِيل from سَعِدَ (saʿida, 'to be fortunate, happy'), root س-ع-د (s-ʿ-d).

سفر.etymology: Verbal/abstract noun سَفَر (safar, 'travel, journey, setting out on a trip'), originally 'unveiling or setting forth into the open country', from the root س-ف-ر (s-f-r).

سقف.etymology: Classical Arabic سَقْف (saqf, 'ceiling, roof, overhead covering'), from the Semitic root س-ق-ف (s-q-f, 'roofing over').

سكت.etymology: Form I verb سَكَتَ (sakata, 'to fall silent, become quiet, stop speaking'), cognate with Hebrew שָׁקַט (šāqaṭ, 'to be quiet, at rest'), root س-ك-ت (s-k-t).

سكر.etymology: Borrowed via Middle Persian *šakar* from Sanskrit *śárkarā* ('gravel, grit, crystallized sugar').
سكر.notes: Medieval Arabic trade carried السكر into European languages, producing Spanish *azúcar*, French *sucre*, and English 'sugar'.

سكن.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šakan- ('to settle, dwell, come to rest'), yielding Classical Arabic سَكَنَ (sakana, 'to live, reside; become still'), root س-ك-ن (s-k-n).

سكّر.etymology: Form II verb سَكَّرَ (sakkara, 'to close, shut, bolt a door; hang up a phone'), inherited from Semitic *s-k-r (cognate with Aramaic סַכֵּר sakkēr and Akkadian sekēru, 'to shut, dam up, block'), root س-ك-ر.

سلاسة.etymology: Abstract noun سَلَاسَة (salāsa, 'smoothness, ease, fluency') on the pattern فَعَالَة from سَلِسَ (salisa, 'to be smooth, easy-flowing, compliant'), root س-ل-س (s-l-s).

سلام.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šalām- ('wholeness, peace, welfare'), yielding Classical Arabic سَلَام (salām, 'peace, greeting; in يَا سَلَام! an exclamation of delight and wonder'), root س-ل-م (s-l-m).

سلامة.etymology: Abstract noun سَلَامَة (salāma, 'safety, soundness, freedom from harm', used in مَعَ السَّلَامَةِ 'goodbye' and الحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ عَلَى السَّلَامَةِ) from سَلِمَ (salima, 'to be safe and whole'), root س-ل-م.

سلة.etymology: Derived from the Semitic root س-ل-ل (s-l-l, 'to pull out, weave reeds'), originally naming a woven reed or wicker market basket.

سلك.etymology: Classical Arabic سِلْك (silk, 'thread, string, cord; drawn metal wire') from سَلَكَ (salaka, 'to thread, pass along a path'), root س-ل-ك (s-l-k).

سلم.etymology: Noun سُلَّم ('ladder, flight of steps; musical scale') from the root س-ل-م ('be safe, ascend safely step by step'), naming the runged wooden ladder because it carries a climber safely upward.

سليم.etymology: Adjective سَلِيم (salīm, 'sound, intact, whole, safe and sound') on the pattern فَعِيل from سَلِمَ (salima, 'to be safe, unblemished'), root س-ل-م (s-l-m).

سلّم.etymology: Form II verb سَلَّمَ (sallama, 'to hand over intact, deliver; greet someone by wishing peace [سَلَام]') from the root س-ل-م (s-l-m).

history.meaning: to deliver safely; greet with peace

سما.etymology: Spoken and lightened Classical form سَمَا (samā, 'sky, heaven') of سَمَاء (samāʾ) via loss of final glottal stop, inherited from Proto-Semitic *šamāy- ('sky, heaven'), root س-م-و (s-m-w, 'to be high, lofty').

سماع.etymology: Form I verbal noun سَمَاع (samāʿ, 'hearing, listening') from سَمِعَ (samiʿa, 'to hear, listen'), root س-م-ع (s-m-ʿ).

سماعة.etymology: Instrumental noun سَمَّاعَة (sammāʿa, 'telephone handset/receiver, earpiece, headphones') on the pattern فَعَّالَة from سَمِعَ (samiʿa, 'to hear'), root س-م-ع (s-m-ʿ).

سمح.etymology: Form I verb سَمَحَ (samaḥa, 'to be magnanimous, allow, permit, excuse', used in the polite formula لَوْ سَمَحْت 'if you please / excuse me') from the root س-م-ح (s-m-ḥ, 'generosity, indulgence').

سمع.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šamaʿ- ('to hear, listen'), yielding Classical Arabic سَمِعَ (samiʿa), root س-م-ع (s-m-ʿ).

سميك.etymology: Adjective سَمِيك (samīk, 'thick, dense') on the pattern فَعِيل from سَمُكَ (samuka, 'to be thick, high'), root س-م-ك (s-m-k).

سمّى.etymology: Form II verb سَمَّى (sammā, 'to name, call by a name'), denominative from اِسْم (ism, 'name', Proto-Semitic *šim-), root س-م-و (s-m-w).

سن.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šinn- ('tooth'), yielding Classical Arabic سِنّ (sinn, 'tooth; by extension, a pointed cog, notch, or screw/pipe thread'), root س-ن-ن (s-n-n).

سنة.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šan-at- ('year'), yielding Classical Arabic سَنَة (sana, plural سِنُونَ / سِنِين sinīn and سَنَوَات sanawāt), root س-ن-و (s-n-w).

سنتيمتر.etymology: Metric measurement loanword borrowed from French centimètre ('one hundredth of a meter', from Latin centum 'hundred' + Greek μέτρον 'measure').

سند.etymology: Form I verb سَنَدَ (sanada, 'to lean, prop up, support against a wall or back'), from the root س-ن-د (s-n-d, 'propping, supporting').

سنوي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective سَنَوِيّ (sanawiyy, 'annual, yearly') formed from the restored triliteral stem of سَنَة (sana, 'year'), root س-ن-و (s-n-w).

سهل.etymology: Adjective سَهْل ('easy, smooth, level') from the root س-ه-ل, which originally described soft, level lowland plains (سَهْل 'plain') free of rugged stones, and by natural metaphor came to mean 'easy, effortless'.

history.meaning: smooth plain; easy (also in أهلا وسهلا 'you have come to level, easy ground')

سهلا.etymology: Accusative noun سَهْلًا (sahlan, '[onto] smooth, easy ground!'), paired with أَهْلًا in the classical welcome أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا (shortened from حَلَلْتَ أَهْلًا وَنَزَلْتَ سَهْلًا, 'you have joined family and stepped onto level ground'), from سَهْل ('level plain, easy', root س-ه-ل).

سهم.etymology: Classical Arabic سَهْم (sahm, 'arrow, dart; lot or share drawn by arrows'), from the root س-ه-م (s-h-m).

سهولة.etymology: Abstract noun سُهُولَة (suhūla, 'ease, smoothness, facility') on the pattern فُعُولَة from سَهُلَ (sahula, 'to be smooth, level, easy'), root س-ه-ل (s-h-l).

سوا.etymology: Spoken Levantine adverb سَوَا (sawā, 'together, side by side'), from Classical سَوَاء (sawāʾ, 'equality, sameness, together') via regular loss of final glottal stop, root س-و-ي (s-w-y, 'to be equal, even').

سوق.etymology: Ancient Semitic trade word (attested in Aramaic *šūqā*, 'street, marketplace'), naming an open-air or covered market.
سوق.notes: Frequently feminine in Arabic usage; plural أسواق.

سيئ.etymology: Adjective سَيِّئ (sayyiʾ, 'bad, poor, unfavorable') on the pattern فَيْعِل from سَاءَ (sāʾa, 'to be bad, grieve, harm'), root س-و-ء (s-w-ʾ).

سياحي.etymology: Nisba adjective from سِيَاحَة (siyāḥa, 'tourism, travel'), from the root س-ي-ح (s-y-ḥ, 'to flow, roam, travel through the land').

سيارة.etymology: Originally the feminine intensive active participle سَيَّارَة (sayyāra) meaning 'caravan, company of travellers constantly on the move' (as in the Quranic 'sayyāratun'), from سَارَ (sāra, 'to travel, move along'); repurposed in modern Arabic to mean 'automobile, car'.

history.meaning: caravan of travellers; wandering planet; (modern) automobile, car

سيارة.notes: A classic example of classical Quranic vocabulary revived in the 20th century for modern technology.

سيرة.etymology: From Classical Arabic سِيرَة (sīra, 'manner of walking, way of life, biography, story'), verbal noun of manner (fiʿla) from سَارَ (sāra, 'to walk, go, conduct oneself'). In Levantine Arabic, used for 'mention, topic of conversation' (as in جاب سيرة 'to bring up a topic').

history.meaning: way of going, conduct, biography, account

سِخِن.etymology: From Classical Arabic سَخُنَ / سَخِنَ (saḵuna / saḵina, 'to be or become hot, warm up'), from the Proto-Semitic root *š-ḫ-n ('to be warm, hot').

history.meaning: to become hot, warm up; to have a fever

شاء.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَاءَ (šāʾa, 'to will, wish, desire'), hollow verb from the root ش-ي-ء (š-y-ʾ), preserved across all spoken Arabic dialects especially in the formula إِنْ شَاءَ اللّٰهُ (ʾin šāʾa llāhu, 'if God wills').

morphemes.meaning: to will, wish; a willed thing

شاحنة.etymology: Feminine active participle شَاحِنَة ('freight truck, lorry') from the root ش-ح-ن ('load cargo, fill a vessel'), coined in modern Arabic from سَيَّارَة شَاحِنَة ('cargo-carrying vehicle').

history.meaning: to load a ship with cargo

شارع.etymology: Active participle of ش-ر-ع (sh-r-', 'to open onto, lead into, set forth a path'), originally 'an open thoroughfare' and today 'street'.
شارع.notes: Takes the quadriliteral broken plural شوارع.

morphemes.meaning: opening a way, setting a path

شاشة.etymology: Originally denoting 'fine white muslin cloth' (from شَاش šāš, wrapped as a turban or hung as a projection sheet for shadow plays and early cinema), which came to mean 'projection screen' and then 'television, computer, or phone screen', or reinforced by French châssis ('frame, screen').

history.meaning: piece of white muslin cloth; projection sheet; screen

شاشة.notes: Initially applied to the white fabric sheet on which early magic-lantern and cinema images were projected.

شاف.etymology: Pan-vernacular Arabic verb for 'to see, look', from Classical Arabic شَافَ (šāfa, Form I hollow verb from ش-و-ف) and تَشَوَّفَ (tašawwafa, 'to gaze down from a height, crane one's neck to look out, polish'), which replaced Classical رَأَى (raʾā) in everyday speech.

history.meaning: to look out from above, gaze, observe; to polish

morphemes.meaning: to look out, gaze from a height, polish

شاف.notes: Cognate with Hebrew שׁוּף (šūp̄) and Aramaic שׁוּף.

شال.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَالَ (šāla, 'to rise, be lifted; to lift up, raise, carry'), hollow verb from the root ش-ي-ل (š-y-l). In Levantine and Egyptian Arabic, the primary verb for 'to lift, carry away, remove'.

شاي.etymology: Ultimately from Sinitic 茶 (chá, 'tea'), reaching Arabic along overland Silk Road trade routes via Persian چای (čây) and Ottoman Turkish çay.
شاي.notes: Languages supplied overland via Central Asia and Persia adopted 'cha/shay' forms, whereas maritime European trade from Fujian adopted 'tea/thé'.

شايف.etymology: Active participle of شَاف (šāf, 'to see, look'), corresponding to Classical شَائِف (šāʾif) with regular vernacular shift of medial glottal stop to yāʾ.

morphemes.meaning: doer or current state of the action

شب.etymology: Levantine and general spoken reflex of Classical Arabic شَابّ (šābb, 'young man, youth'), active participle of شَبَّ (šabba, 'to grow up, enter youth, blaze up'), shortened from long vowel before geminate consonant.

history.meaning: young man, youth in the prime of life

morphemes.meaning: to grow up, blaze with youth and vigor

شباك.etymology: From the root ش-ب-ك (sh-b-k, 'to interlace, entwine like a net'), originally naming the latticework grille or mashrabiya fitted across a window opening, and in Levantine Arabic the everyday word for 'window'.
شباك.notes: Compare Standard Arabic نافذة ('opening'); spoken Jordanian uses شباك (plural شبابيك) for windows and wooden shutters alike.

شبك.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَبَك (šabak, collective of شَبَكَة šabaka, 'net, lattice, mesh, grid, wire rack'), from the root ش-ب-ك (š-b-k, 'to interlace, entwine, mesh together').

شتا.etymology: From Classical Arabic شِتَاء (šitāʾ, 'winter; rainy season; rain') with regular vernacular loss of final hamza. In the Levant, where rain falls almost exclusively in winter, شتا means both 'winter' and 'rain'.

morphemes.meaning: winter, passing the winter, winter rain

شتوية.etymology: Feminine nisba noun شَتْوِيَّة (šatwiyya) derived from شِتَاء (šitāʾ, 'winter, rain'), used in Levantine Arabic to mean 'the winter season' or 'a heavy rainstorm / downpour'.

morphemes.meaning: season or bout of an event

شجر.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَجَر (šajar, collective noun for 'trees, woody plants, shrubs'), from the root ش-ج-ر (š-j-r, 'to branch out, intertwine').

شجرة.etymology: Singulative noun (ism waḥda) formed by adding -a (ـة) to the collective شَجَر (šajar, 'trees'), denoting 'a single tree'.

شخص.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَخْص (šaḵṣ, 'person, individual, bodily silhouette seen from afar'), from شَخَصَ (šaḵaṣa, 'to rise up, loom into view, stare fixedly').

morphemes.meaning: rising into view, distinct figure, person

شد.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَدَّ (šadda, 'to pull taut, bind tightly, fasten, strengthen'), geminate verb from the root ش-د-د (š-d-d, 'tightness, firmness, intensity').

history.meaning: to pull tight, bind fast, make firm

شرب.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَرِبَ (šariba, 'to drink, absorb'), from the Semitic root ش-ر-ب (š-r-b, 'drinking, absorbing liquid').
شرب.notes: Source of English 'sherbet', 'sorbet', and 'syrup' (via شَرَاب šarāb 'beverage').

شرح.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَرَحَ (šaraḥa, 'to slice open meat, lay bare, expand, explain, comment upon'), from the root ش-ر-ح (š-r-ḥ). The sense 'to explain' developed metaphorically from 'opening up or laying out something hidden' (as in Quranic أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ لَكَ صَدْرَكَ 'Did We not expand for you your breast?').

history.meaning: to cut open in slices, lay open, expand, explain

شرشف.etymology: From Classical and post-Classical Arabic شَرْشَف (šaršaf, 'bedsheet, tablecloth'), borrowed from Persian چادرشب (čādar-šab, literally 'night-sheet / night-cloth') and reinforced in Levantine via Ottoman Turkish çarşaf.

شرط.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَرْط (šarṭ, 'condition, stipulation, proviso; incision or sign'), from the root ش-ر-ط (š-r-ط, 'to make a binding mark or stipulation, slit').

morphemes.meaning: making a mark or binding stipulation, slitting

شريحة.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَرِيحَة (šarīḥa, 'thin slice of meat, long flat strip, slat, louvre'), on the pattern فَعِيلَة (faʿīla, passive/resultative sense 'that which is sliced flat') from شَرَحَ (šaraḥa, 'to slice open, spread flat').

morphemes.meaning: something sliced into a thin flat strip

شريطة.etymology: Singulative of شَرِيط (šarīṭ, 'braided cord, tape, strip, ribbon'), from the root ش-ر-ط (š-r-ṭ, 'to slit into strips, braid palm-leaf cords').

شريك.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَرِيك (šarīk, 'partner, associate, sharer'), on the pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from شَرِكَ (šarika, 'to share, participate in').

شرّف.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَرَّفَ (šarrafa, 'to honour, exalt, ennoble'), Form II causative of شَرُفَ (šarufa, 'to be high-born, noble, elevated'). Widely used in polite hospitality formulas such as شرّفتنا (šarraftnā, 'you have honoured us [with your visit]').

شعرة.etymology: Singulative noun (ism waḥda) شَعْرَة (šaʿra, 'a single hair; a hair's breadth'), formed from the collective شَعْر (šaʿr, 'hair'), from Proto-Semitic *śaʿr- ('hair').

شعلة.etymology: From Classical Arabic شُعْلَة (šuʿla, 'flame, firebrand, torch; pilot light'), from شَعَلَ / أَشْعَلَ (šaʿala / ʾašʿala, 'to kindle, ignite, blaze').

شغال.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَغَّال (šaḡḡāl, 'hard-working, busy, active'), intensive adjective on the pattern فَعَّال (faʿʿāl) from شَغَلَ (šaḡala, 'to occupy, work'); in spoken Arabic, also used for machines and appliances meaning 'working, running, switched on'.

شغل.etymology: From Classical Arabic شُغْل (šuḡl, 'occupation, work, business, task'), from the root ش-غ-ل (š-ḡ-l, 'to occupy, keep busy').

شغلة.etymology: Instance/singulative noun شَغْلَة (šaḡla) from شُغْل (šuḡl, 'work, occupation'), meaning 'a single job, task, matter' and broadened in Levantine Arabic to mean 'thing, item, affair'.

history.meaning: a piece of work, task, matter, thing

شغّل.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَغَّلَ (šaḡḡala, 'to set to work, employ, occupy'), Form II causative of شَغَلَ (šaḡala); in modern Arabic, also 'to turn on, start up, operate (a machine or appliance)'.

history.meaning: to keep busy, put to work; to start up, operate

morphemes.meaning: causative: to make work or run

شق.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَقَّ (šaqqa, 'to split, cleave, crack open, tear'), geminate verb from the root ش-ق-ق (š-q-q, 'splitting, cleaving').

شكر.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَكَرَ (šakara, 'to thank, praise, show gratitude to'), from the Semitic root ش-ك-ر (š-k-r, 'gratitude, bountifulness, acknowledgment of favour').

history.meaning: to thank, be grateful to, praise

شكرا.etymology: From Classical Arabic شُكْرًا (šukran, 'thank you, thanks'), the adverbial accusative (mafʿūl muṭlaq) of the verbal noun شُكْر (šukr, 'gratitude, thanking'), literally '[I offer you] thanks'.

morphemes.meaning: cognate accusative used as an exclamation

شكل.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَكْل (šakl, 'shape, form, figure, likeness, appearance, kind'), from the root ش-ك-ل (š-k-l, 'to form, fashion, resemble, bind').

شلح.etymology: Levantine verb شَلَحَ (šalaḥa, 'to take off, strip off [clothes or shoes], throw off'), inherited through an Aramaic substrate from Aramaic שְׁלַח / ܫܠܚ (šlaḥ, 'to strip off clothes, shed skin, send'), cognate with Classical Arabic سَلَخَ (salaḵa, 'to skin, strip off').

history.meaning: to strip off, take off (clothing or footwear)

شم.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَمَّ (šamma, 'to smell, sniff, inhale an odour'), geminate verb from the root ش-م-م (š-m-m).

morphemes.meaning: smelling, sniffing; highness of the nose

شمال.etymology: From Classical Arabic شِمَال (šimāl, 'left hand, left side') and شَمَال (šamāl, 'north, north wind'), from Proto-Semitic *śimʾāl- ('left side; north', since when facing the rising sun in the east, north lies to one's left).

شمس.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šamš- ('sun'), grammatically feminine in Arabic and famously the model word for 'sun letters' (الحروف الشمسية), since الشَّمْس assimilates the l of ال- into ash-shams.
شمس.notes: Contrasts with القمر ('the moon'), model for non-assimilating moon letters.

شنتة.etymology: Borrowed into Levantine and Egyptian Arabic from Ottoman Turkish *çanta* ('bag, pouch, suitcase').
شنتة.notes: In Amman شنتة (plural شناتي) covers handbags, backpacks, and travel suitcases.

شنكل.etymology: Levantine and Egyptian شَنْكَل (šankal, 'hook, catch, window latch'), borrowed via Ottoman Turkish çengel ('hook, grappling iron') from Persian چنگل / چنگال (čangal / čangāl, 'claw, talon, hook').

شهر.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَهْر (šahr, 'month; new moon'), from the root ش-ه-ر (š-h-r, 'to make conspicuous, proclaim') or Proto-Semitic *śahr- ('moon, crescent moon, month'), because the lunar month begins when the new crescent moon becomes visible.

morphemes.meaning: moon, month; making conspicuous or famous

شهري.etymology: Formed from شهر ('month') plus the relational nisba suffix ـي (-iyy), yielding 'monthly'.
شهري.notes: شهر itself is an inherited Semitic time noun originally tied to the new moon.

شو.etymology: Levantine interrogative pronoun شُو (šū, 'what?'), grammaticalized by phonetic reduction from Classical Arabic أَيُّ شَيْءٍ هُوَ (ʾayyu šayʾin huwa, 'what thing is it?') via intermediate *ʾēš-hu > *š-hū > šū.
شو.notes: Part of the pan-Arabic family of interrogatives derived from أَيُّ شَيْءٍ (compare ايش ʾēš, شنو šnū).

شوربة.etymology: From Ottoman Turkish çorba ('soup'), itself from Persian شوربا (šōrbā, 'broth, stew', from شور šōr 'salty, brackish' + با bā 'broth, pottage'), though popular folk etymology often connects it to Arabic شَرِبَ (šariba, 'to drink') and شَرْبَة (šarba, 'a drink, draught').

شوفير.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century from French chauffeur ('motorcar driver', originally 'stoker, fireman of a steam engine', from chauffer 'to heat').

شوي.etymology: Levantine and Gulf Arabic شْوَيّ (šwayy, 'a little, a bit, a moment'), from Classical Arabic شُوَيّ (šuwayy), the regular diminutive (فُعَيْل fuʿayl) of شَيْء (šayʾ, 'a thing'), literally 'a little thing'.

history.meaning: a little thing, a small bit (diminutive of شَيْء)

شوية.etymology: Feminine diminutive شُوَيَّة (šuwayya, 'a little bit of, a small amount of') from شَيْء (šayʾ, 'thing'); in Levantine Arabic, used especially in construct before a following noun (e.g. شوية مي 'a little bit of water').

history.meaning: a small bit, a little portion of

شي.etymology: Spoken Arabic reflex of Classical Arabic شَيْء (šayʾ, 'thing, something; around/approximately'), with loss of final hamza and monophthongization or raising to šī / šay.

history.meaning: thing, something (originally verbal noun of شَاءَ 'to will')

morphemes.meaning: to will, wish; a willed thing

شيش.etymology: Levantine and Egyptian شِيش (šīš, 'slatted wooden window shutters, Venetian blinds, laths, bars, skewer'), borrowed via Ottoman Turkish şiş ('skewer, rapier, lath') and Persian شيش (šīš, 'rod, lath, skewer').

شيف.etymology: Borrowed from French chef (short for chef de cuisine, 'head of the kitchen') and English chef, ultimately from Latin caput ('head').

شَبَك.etymology: From Classical Arabic شَبَكَ (šabaka, 'to interlace, entwine, fasten together, hook into'), from the root ش-ب-ك (š-b-k). In modern usage, also means 'to plug in, clip together, connect'.

history.meaning: to interlace, mesh, fasten or hook together

صاب.etymology: Spoken Arabic reflex of Classical Arabic أَصَابَ (ʾaṣāba, 'to hit the mark, strike, befall, afflict') merged with Form I صَابَ (ṣāba, 'to pour down, descend directly upon a target'), from the hollow root ص-و-ب (ṣ-w-b, 'going straight to the mark').

history.meaning: to hit the mark, strike, touch, befall

morphemes.meaning: going straight to a target, hitting the mark

صابون.etymology: Early Mediterranean Wanderwort entering Arabic via Aramaic *ṣābūnā* from Late Latin *sāpō* ('soap'), then carried by Levantine olive-oil soapmakers back across medieval trade networks.
صابون.notes: Levantine olive-oil soap (from Nablus, Aleppo, and Salt) has been famous for over a millennium.

صاحب.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَاحِب (ṣāḥib, 'companion, friend, associate; owner, master of'), active participle of صَحِبَ (ṣaḥiba, 'to accompany, associate with').
صاحب.notes: Borrowed into Hindi/Urdu and English as 'sahib'.

صادق.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَادِق (ṣādiq, 'truthful, honest, sincere, genuine'), active participle of صَدَقَ (ṣadaqa, 'to speak the truth, be true and sincere').

صار.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَارَ (ṣāra, 'to become, come to be, happen, begin to'), one of the classical 'sisters of kāna' (أخوات كان), from the hollow root ص-ي-ر (ṣ-y-r, 'coming to a state or destination').

history.meaning: to become, turn into, come to pass

morphemes.meaning: reaching a state, becoming, ultimate outcome

صارم.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَارِم (ṣārim, 'strict, stern, resolute; sharp-cutting sword'), active participle of صَرَمَ (ṣarama, 'to cut off cleanly, sever decisively').

صافي.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَافٍ / الصَّافِي (ṣāfin / aṣ-ṣāfī, 'clear, pure, unclouded, net'), active participle of صَفَا (ṣafā, 'to be clear, pure, cloudless, free of sediment').

morphemes.meaning: being in a clear or pure state

صب.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَبَّ (ṣabba, 'to pour out, pour forth, cast in a mould'), geminate verb from the root ص-ب-ب (ṣ-b-b).

صباح.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَبَاح (ṣabāḥ, 'morning, daybreak, forenoon'), from the root ص-ب-ح (ṣ-b-ḥ, 'to shine brightly, dawn, greet in the morning').

صباحي.etymology: Nisba adjective صَبَاحِيّ (ṣabāḥiyy, 'morning [adj.], matutinal') formed from صَبَاح (ṣabāḥ, 'morning') with the relational suffix -ī (ـِيّ).

history.meaning: of or relating to the morning

صبح.etymology: From Classical Arabic صُبْح (ṣubḥ, 'dawn, daybreak, morning'), from the root ص-ب-ح (ṣ-b-ḥ, 'to shine, gleam, dawn').

صبر.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَبْر (ṣabr, 'patience, endurance, steadfastness, self-restraint'), verbal noun of صَبَرَ (ṣabara, 'to be patient, endure steadfastly, bind').

صبّح.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَبَّحَ (ṣabbaḥa, 'to greet someone in the morning, visit or come upon at dawn'), Form II denominative verb from صُبْح / صَبَاح (ṣubḥ / ṣabāḥ, 'morning').

history.meaning: to bid good morning; to enter upon the morning

morphemes.meaning: denominative: to greet or act in the morning

صح.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَحَّ (ṣaḥḥa, 'to be sound, true, valid, correct; to be healthy'), geminate verb from the root ص-ح-ح (ṣ-ḥ-ḥ); used in spoken Arabic both as a verb ('to come true, be possible') and as an adjective/interjection ('right!, true, correct').

history.meaning: to be sound, true, correct, authentic

صحة.etymology: From Classical Arabic صِحَّة (ṣiḥḥa, 'health, soundness, validity, correctness'), verbal noun of صَحَّ (ṣaḥḥa, 'to be healthy, sound, whole'). Used both for physical health and in polite expressions like صحتين (ṣaḥtēn, 'bon appétit / twice health!').

صحن.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَحْن (ṣaḥn, 'broad shallow dish, plate, open courtyard'), from root ص-ح-ن denoting a flat, open basin or saucer.

صحو.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَحْو (ṣaḥw, 'cloudlessness, clear sunny sky;清醒/waking state after sleep or intoxication'), verbal noun of صَحَا (ṣaḥā, 'to become clear and cloudless; to wake up, sober up').

history.meaning: clearness of the sky; waking consciousness

morphemes.meaning: clearing of clouds; waking up, becoming alert

صحى.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَحَا / صَحِيَ (ṣaḥā / ṣaḥiya, 'to wake up, regain consciousness, sober up; for the sky to clear of clouds'), from the root ص-ح-و (ṣ-ḥ-w).

history.meaning: to wake up, become alert; to clear up (of weather)

morphemes.meaning: clearing of clouds; waking up, becoming alert

صحّى.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَحَّى (ṣaḥḥā), Form II causative of صَحَا (ṣaḥā, 'to wake up'), meaning 'to wake someone up, rouse from sleep'.

morphemes.meaning: causative: to cause someone to wake up

صخر.etymology: Collective noun صَخْر ('solid rock, boulders', singulative صَخْرَة) from the Semitic root ص-خ-ر, evoking immovable mountain bedrock—hence the proverbial simile ثابت متل الصخر ('steady as rock').

صدفة.etymology: From Classical and Modern Standard Arabic صُدْفَة (ṣudfa, 'coincidence, chance encounter'), related to صَادَفَ (ṣādafa, 'to come across by chance, happen upon, coincide with'), from the root ص-د-ف (ṣ-d-ف, 'to turn, meet unexpectedly').

morphemes.meaning: meeting by chance, turning towards or away

صدق.etymology: From Classical Arabic صِدْق (ṣidq, 'truth, truthfulness, sincerity, honesty'), verbal noun of صَدَقَ (ṣadaqa, 'to speak the truth, be true').

صدمة.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَدْمَة (ṣadma, 'collision, impact, blow, shock'), noun of instance (ism marra) from صَدَمَ (ṣadama, 'to strike violently against, collide with, shock').

history.meaning: a single blow, collision, impact, shock

صدى.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَدًى (ṣadan, 'echo, reverberation; extreme thirst'), from the root ص-د-ي (ṣ-d-y, 'to echo, reverberate, respond to a voice').

صدّق.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَدَّقَ (ṣaddaqa, 'to believe someone, accept as true, confirm, ratify'), Form II declarative/estimative verb from صَدَقَ (ṣadaqa, 'to tell the truth'), literally 'to deem someone truthful'.

morphemes.meaning: estimative: to regard as true, believe

صراحة.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَرَاحَة (ṣarāḥa, 'pureness, unmixedness, frankness, openness, candour'), verbal noun of صَرُحَ (ṣaruḥa, 'to be pure, unmixed, clear, explicit, frank').

صرخ.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَرَخَ (ṣaraḵa, 'to cry out loudly, shout, scream, call for help'), from the Semitic root ص-ر-خ (ṣ-r-ḵ, 'crying out, shouting').

صريح.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَرِيح (ṣarīḥ, 'pure, unmixed, clear, explicit, frank, candid'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from صَرُحَ (ṣaruḥa, 'to be pure, clear, unmixed').

morphemes.meaning: having the quality of clarity and frankness

صعب.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَعْب (ṣaʿb, 'hard, difficult, refractory, stubborn [originally of an unbroken camel or steep terrain]'), verbal adjective from صَعُبَ (ṣaʿuba, 'to be hard, difficult').

صغر.etymology: From Classical Arabic صِغَر / صُغْر (ṣiḡar / ṣuḡr, 'smallness, littleness, youth, young age'), verbal noun of صَغُرَ (ṣaḡura, 'to be small, little, young').

صغير.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَغِير (ṣaḡīr, 'small, little, young'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from صَغُرَ (ṣaḡura, 'to be small, young').

صف.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَفّ (ṣaff, 'row, line, rank, queue; classroom/grade'), verbal noun of صَفَّ (ṣaffa, 'to set in a row, align, arrange in order').

morphemes.meaning: arranging in a row or line

صفحة.etymology: Instance/surface noun from root ص-ف-ح (ṣ-f-ḥ, 'to flatten out, broaden a surface'): originally the flat side of a blade, cheek, or leaf of parchment, hence 'page'.

history.meaning: flat side; face of a sheet; page

صفّق.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَفَّقَ (ṣaffaqa, 'to clap the hands, applaud; to flap wings'), Form II intensive of صَفَقَ (ṣafaqa, 'to strike sharply with a flat sound, slap, slam shut').

history.meaning: to clap the hands repeatedly, applaud

morphemes.meaning: striking flat surfaces together, clapping, slapping

صلّح.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَلَّحَ (ṣallaḥa, 'to put right, repair, mend, restore to good order'), Form II causative of صَلَحَ (ṣalaḥa, 'to be good, sound, in proper order, suitable').

history.meaning: to repair, mend, put in order

morphemes.meaning: causative: to make sound or functional again

صمام.etymology: From Classical Arabic صِمَام (ṣimām, 'stopper, plug of a flask; valve'), on the instrument pattern فِعَال (fiʿāl) from صَمَّ (ṣamma, 'to plug, stopper up tightly, be solid or deaf').

morphemes.meaning: device that plugs or regulates flow

صمّم.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَمَّمَ (ṣammama, 'to resolve firmly, be determined; [modern] to design, plan'), Form II of صَمَّ (ṣamma, 'to be solid, firm'); the modern sense 'to design' developed from 'giving firm, definitive form to a plan'.

history.meaning: to determine firmly, resolve; (modern) to design

morphemes.meaning: intensive: to fix firmly or design

صندوق.etymology: From Classical Arabic صُنْدُوق / صَنْدُوق (ṣundūq / ṣandūq, 'box, chest, trunk, coffer, cash box'), an early cultural loanword (likely via Byzantine Greek σάνδυξ / σενδούκιον or Aramaic/Iranian) fully integrated into Arabic morphology with broken plural صَنَادِيق (ṣanādīq).
صندوق.notes: Re-borrowed from Arabic into Turkish (sandık), Balkan languages, and Spanish (zandoque).

صنفرة.etymology: From Arabic صَنْفَرَة / سَنْفَرَة (ṣanfara / sanfara, 'sanding, abrasion; emery, sandpaper [ورق صنفرة]'), derived from medieval Arabic سَنْبَاذَج (sanbāḏaj, 'emery stone, abrasive corundum', from Persian سنباده sunbāda) or Ottoman Turkish zımpara ('emery paper, sandpaper').

صوت.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَوْت (ṣawt, 'sound, voice, noise; vote'), from the root ص-و-ت (ṣ-w-t, 'to make a sound, ring out, call').

صوتي.etymology: Nisba adjective صَوْتِيّ (ṣawtiyy, 'vocal, acoustic, audio, phonetic') formed from صَوْت (ṣawt, 'sound, voice') with the relational suffix -ī (ـِيّ).

history.meaning: relating to sound or voice; acoustic, vocal

صوتيات.etymology: Feminine plural substantive صَوْتِيَّات (ṣawtiyyāt, 'acoustics, phonetics, audio equipment'), formed as the feminine plural of the nisba adjective صَوْتِيّ (ṣawtiyy, 'acoustic, vocal') from صَوْت (ṣawt, 'sound').

morphemes.meaning: field of study or class of phenomena

صورة.etymology: From the root ص-و-ر (ṣ-w-r), expressing shaping, forming, and depicting; extended from 'form, image, likeness' to modern drawings and photographs.

صوف.etymology: From Classical Arabic صُوف (ṣūf, 'wool, fleece'), collective noun from the root ص-و-ف (ṣ-w-f). Commonly held by classical Arab lexicographers to be the source of صُوفِيّ (ṣūfī, 'Sufi mystic', from the coarse woollen garment worn by early ascetics).

صول.etymology: Musical note name صُول (ṣōl, 'Sol, the fifth note G of the diatonic scale'), borrowed from French and Italian solfège sol.

history.meaning: fifth note of the musical scale (G)

صون.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَوْن (ṣawn, 'preserving, safeguarding, protecting from harm or dishonour'), verbal noun of صَانَ (ṣāna, 'to guard, preserve, keep safe').

صيانة.etymology: From Classical Arabic صِيَانَة (ṣiyāna, 'preservation, safeguarding, upkeep, maintenance'), second verbal noun (on pattern فِعَالَة fiʿāla) of صَانَ (ṣāna, 'to preserve, guard, maintain').

صيدلية.etymology: From Classical and Modern Standard Arabic صَيْدَلِيَّة (ṣaydaliyya, 'pharmacy, apothecary shop'), derived from صَيْدَلِيّ (ṣaydaliyy, 'pharmacist, apothecary') and صَيْدَلَة (ṣaydala, 'pharmacology'), originally connected to صَنْدَل (ṣandal, 'sandalwood, aromatic drugs traded from India').

صيف.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَيْف (ṣayf, 'summer'), from the Proto-Semitic root *ṣ-y-p ('warm season, summer').

صينية.etymology: Substantivized feminine nisba صِينِيَّة ('serving tray, round baking pan', plural صَوَانِي) from الصِّين ('China'): originally naming fine imported Chinese porcelain platters, and later extended across the Levant to brass, copper, and oven trays.

morphemes.meaning: Chinese platter -> serving or baking tray

ضاع.etymology: From Classical Arabic ضَاعَ (ḍāʿa, 'to be lost, perish, go to waste'), hollow verb from the root ض-ي-ع (ḍ-y-ʿ, 'loss, perishing, going astray').

history.meaning: to be lost, go astray, go to waste

ضايق.etymology: From Classical Arabic ضَايَقَ (ḍāyaqa, 'to hem in, press hard upon, crowd, annoy, bother'), Form III of ضَاقَ (ḍāqa, 'to be narrow, tight, constricted').

morphemes.meaning: associative: to press upon or bother someone

ضايل.etymology: Levantine active participle ضَايِل (ḍāyil, 'remaining, left over, staying'), formed on the hollow active participle pattern from ضَلّ (ḍall, 'to stay, remain'), itself the vernacular reflex of Classical ظَلَّ (ẓalla, 'to remain, continue').

ضبط.etymology: From Classical Arabic ضَبَطَ (ḍabaṭa, 'to hold fast, keep under firm control, regulate, adjust accurately, set [an alarm or instrument]'), from the root ض-ب-ط (ḍ-b-ṭ, 'firmness, exactness, control').

history.meaning: to hold firmly, regulate, adjust accurately

ضجة.etymology: From Classical Arabic ضَجَّة (ḍajja, 'clamour, outcry, tumult, noisy bustle'), noun from ضَجَّ (ḍajja, 'to cry out tumultuously, make an uproar').

ضرب.etymology: From Classical Arabic ضَرَبَ (ḍaraba, 'to strike, hit, beat, coin money, set forth a proverb'), one of the most polysemous core verbs of Arabic, from the root ض-ر-ب (ḍ-r-b); in modern spoken usage, also 'to blow (of a fuse)' or 'to ring/call'.

ضربة.etymology: From Classical Arabic ضَرْبَة (ḍarba, 'a single blow, strike, stroke, beat'), noun of instance (ism marra) from ضَرَبَ (ḍaraba, 'to strike, hit').

ضعف.etymology: From Classical Arabic ضِعْف (ḍiʿf, 'the like amount again, double, twofold'), from the root ض-ع-ف (ḍ-ʿ-f, 'to double, fold over; [with ḍamma/fatḥa ضَعْف/ضُعْف] weakness').

history.meaning: double, twice the amount, a like fold

morphemes.meaning: multiple or fold of a quantity

ضغط.etymology: From Classical Arabic ضَغْط (ḍaḡṭ, 'pressing, squeezing against, compression, pressure, stress'), verbal noun of ضَغَطَ (ḍaḡaṭa, 'to press, squeeze tightly').

ضل.etymology: Levantine and Egyptian reflex of Classical Arabic ظَلَّ (ẓalla, 'to remain, continue doing, stay throughout the day'), with the regular urban vernacular merger of interdental ظ (ẓ) into emphatic dāl ض (ḍ).

history.meaning: to remain, stay, continue in a state

ضل.notes: Distinct in origin from Classical ضَلَّ (ḍalla, 'to go astray'), though spelled identically in vernacular writing.

ضهر.etymology: Levantine and Egyptian reflex of Classical Arabic ظُهْر (ẓuhr, 'noon, midday', when the sun reaches its highest prominence) and ظَهْر (ẓahr, 'back'), showing the regular vernacular merger of Classical ظ (ẓ) into ض (ḍ).

ضو.etymology: Spoken Arabic reflex of Classical Arabic ضَوْء (ḍawʾ, 'light, brightness, glow; lamp'), from ضَاءَ (ḍāʾa, 'to shine, be bright'), with regular vernacular loss of final hamza.

ضوّى.etymology: From Classical Arabic ضَوَّأَ (ḍawwaʾa, 'to light up, illuminate, kindle a lamp'), Form II causative from the root ض-و-ء (ḍ-w-ʾ, 'light, shining'), reshaped as a final-weak verb ضَوَّى (ḍawwā) after the regular loss of final hamza.

history.meaning: to light up, illuminate, turn on a light

morphemes.meaning: causative: to cause to shine or light up

ضيافة.etymology: From Classical Arabic ضِيَافَة (ḍiyāfa, 'hospitality, entertainment of guests'), verbal noun of ضَافَ / أَضَافَ (ḍāfa / ʾaḍāfa, 'to stay as a guest; to receive and host a guest').

morphemes.meaning: inclining towards for shelter, being or hosting a guest

ضيف.etymology: From Classical Arabic ضَيْف (ḍayf, 'guest, visitor'), originally the verbal noun of ضَافَ (ḍāfa, 'to incline towards someone for shelter and lodging, alight as a guest').

morphemes.meaning: alighting for shelter, being a guest

ضيق.etymology: From Classical Arabic ضَيِّق (ḍayyiq, 'narrow, tight, cramped, constricted') and ضِيق (ḍīq, 'narrowness, tightness, distress'), from ضَاقَ (ḍāqa, 'to be narrow, tight').

ضيّع.etymology: From Classical Arabic ضَيَّعَ (ḍayyaʿa, 'to lose, misplace, squander, waste'), Form II causative of ضَاعَ (ḍāʿa, 'to be lost, perish').

history.meaning: to lose, cause to be lost, waste

morphemes.meaning: causative: to cause something to be lost

ضيّق.etymology: From Classical Arabic ضَيَّقَ (ḍayyaqa, 'to make narrow, tighten, constrict'), Form II causative of ضَاقَ (ḍāqa, 'to be narrow, tight').

morphemes.meaning: causative: to make narrow or tight

طابق.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَابَق / طَابِق (ṭābaq / ṭābiq, 'storey, floor of a building; large flat cover or baking pan'), from the root ط-ب-ق (ṭ-b-q, 'to cover, match layer upon layer, correspond').

history.meaning: layer, storey, floor of a building

طازة.etymology: Colloquial Levantine and Egyptian طَازَة (ṭāza, 'fresh, newly made'), borrowed via Ottoman Turkish taze ('fresh, young, new') from Persian تازه (tāza, 'fresh, new, tender'), a doublet of the earlier Classical borrowing طَازَج (ṭāzaj).

طازج.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَازَج (ṭāzaj, 'fresh, newly picked or baked'), an early borrowing from Middle Persian tāzag (modern Persian تازه tāza, 'fresh, new, young') with regular Arabic rendering of Middle Persian final -g as -j (ج).
طازج.notes: Doublet of the later Ottoman-mediated colloquial form طازة (ṭāza).

طال.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَالَ (ṭāla, 'to be long; to reach out to, extend one's hand to reach'), hollow verb from the root ط-و-ل (ṭ-w-l, 'length, tallness, reach'). In Levantine Arabic, transitive طال means 'to reach [something on a high shelf]'.

history.meaning: to be long; to reach, extend to

طالع.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَالِع (ṭāliʿ, 'rising, ascending, coming out, going up'), active participle of طَلَعَ (ṭalaʿa, 'to rise, ascend, emerge').

morphemes.meaning: currently rising, going up, or going out

طاولة.etymology: Levantine Arabic borrowing via Ottoman Turkish *tavla* or Mediterranean Romance *tavola* (from Latin *tabula*, 'board, plank, table').
طاولة.notes: Everyday word for a dining or café table across Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, and Palestine.

طباشير.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَبَاشِير (ṭabāšīr, 'chalk; originally bamboo siliceous concretion used in medicine'), borrowed from Persian تباشیر (tabāšīr), ultimately from Sanskrit त्वक्षीर (tvakṣīra, 'bamboo manna / bark-milk').

history.meaning: chalk; white mineral or bamboo concretion

طبعا.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَبْعًا (ṭabʿan, 'naturally, of course, certainly'), the adverbial accusative of طَبْع (ṭabʿ, 'nature, innate disposition, imprint'), from طَبَعَ (ṭabaʿa, 'to stamp, imprint, fashion by nature').

morphemes.meaning: in accordance with nature; of course

طبقة.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَبَقَة (ṭabaqa, 'layer, stratum, coat [of paint], class, level, storey'), from the root ط-ب-ق (ṭ-b-q, 'to cover, place layer upon layer, match').

طبلية.etymology: From post-Classical and Levantine/Egyptian Arabic طَبْلِيَّة (ṭabliyya, 'low round wooden table, low wooden stool or tray-table'), derived from طَبْلَة (ṭabla, 'flat wooden tray, drumhead') and reinforced by Late Latin/Byzantine Greek tabula / ταβλίον ('board, low table').

history.meaning: low wooden table or stool, flat wooden stand

طبيعي.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَبِيعِيّ (ṭabīʿiyy, 'natural, normal, physical'), nisba adjective from طَبِيعَة (ṭabīʿa, 'nature, innate character'), from the root ط-ب-ع (ṭ-b-ʿ, 'to stamp, imprint').

طرف.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَرَف (ṭaraf, 'extremity, edge, tip, border, corner, end, party'), from the root ط-ر-ف (ṭ-r-f, 'extremity, blinking the edge of the eyelid').

morphemes.meaning: edge, extremity, tip, blinking the eye

طريق.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَرِيق (ṭarīq, 'road, way, path'), on the pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl, passive sense 'that which is trodden upon by feet and hooves') from طَرَقَ (ṭaraqa, 'to beat, tread upon, knock, travel by night').

morphemes.meaning: that which is beaten or trodden by travellers

طريقة.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَرِيقَة (ṭarīqa, 'way, method, manner, procedure, style; Sufi order'), feminine/singulative of طَرِيق (ṭarīq, 'road, path'), from طَرَقَ (ṭaraqa, 'to tread a path, beat').

طعم.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَعْم (ṭaʿm, 'taste, flavour, savour'), from the Proto-Semitic root *ṭ-ʿ-m ('to taste, perceive flavour, eat').

طفى.etymology: Spoken Arabic reflex of Classical Arabic طَفِئَ (ṭafiʾa, 'to go out, be extinguished [of fire or light]') and its causative أَطْفَأَ (ʾaṭfaʾa, 'to put out, extinguish, switch off'), merged into a final-weak verb طَفَى (ṭafā) through loss of final hamza.

history.meaning: to go out, be extinguished; to extinguish, switch off

morphemes.meaning: extinguishing fire or light, going out
to go out or put out

طق.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَقَّ (ṭaqqa, 'to crack, pop, snap, burst with a sharp sound'), onomatopoeic geminate root ط-ق-ق (ṭ-q-q) imitating a sharp clicking, snapping, or popping sound; also used as an interjection ('pop!, click!, crack!').

history.meaning: to make a sharp cracking, popping, or clicking sound

طقة.etymology: Noun of instance طَقَّة (ṭaqqa, 'a single pop, click, snap, crack') from the onomatopoeic verb طَقَّ (ṭaqqa, 'to pop, click, crack').

history.meaning: a single click, pop, or crack

طقس.etymology: From Christian and Classical Arabic طَقْس (ṭaqs, 'order, liturgical rite; state of the atmosphere, weather'), borrowed via Syriac ܛܟܣܐ (ṭaksā, 'order, arrangement, rule') from Ancient Greek τάξις (táxis, 'arrangement, order, disposition [including of the heavens and atmosphere]').

طلب.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَلَبَ (ṭalaba, 'to seek, ask for, request, order') and its verbal noun طَلَب (ṭalab, 'request, order, demand'), from the root ط-ل-ب (ṭ-l-b).

history.meaning: to seek, request, ask for; a request or order

morphemes.part: فَعَلَ / فَعَل (Form I verb and verbal noun)

طلع.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَلَعَ (ṭalaʿa, 'to rise [of the sun], ascend, climb up, come out, appear, turn out to be'), from the root ط-ل-ع (ṭ-l-ʿ).

history.meaning: to rise, ascend, emerge, come out

طلى.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَلَى (ṭalā, 'to coat, daub, paint, overlay or plate a surface'), defective verb from the root ط-ل-ي (ṭ-l-y).

morphemes.meaning: coating, painting, smearing over a surface

طلّع.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَلَّعَ (ṭallaʿa, 'to raise up, bring out, carry up; to look closely at'), Form II intensive/causative of طَلَعَ (ṭalaʿa, 'to rise, come out'); in Levantine Arabic, used both for 'to take out / carry up' and (often via اتطلّع) 'to look at'.

history.meaning: to bring out, carry up; to gaze or look at

morphemes.meaning: causative/intensive: to bring up or direct one's gaze
